To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the percentage of PC is increased in the presence of exogenous PG; (2) PG is synthesized from exogenously provided PI by a mechanism that involves a PI 4-kinase and PI 4-P 5-kinase; and (3) the PI 4- and PI 4- 5-kinases are activated by cAMP.
The percentage of PG increases at the expense of PI during the maturation of fetal lung type II cells.
the synthesis of PG and PI is regulated in opposite manners by cAMP and Ca2+.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of phospholipid synthesis in alveoli type II cells.
the regulation of the synthesis of the major phospholipids, PC, PG, and PI, in the alveolar type I1 cell.
the regulation of PG synthesis in the adult lung, and the role of PI and PC in this regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the switch-over from PG to PI synthesis is not understood and that the mechanism is not known.

the switch from PI to PG is not due to an increase in the activity of the PG synthetase, and that the decrease in PI synthesis is not due to a decrease in the activity of CTP: phosphocholine cytidyltransferase.
the regulation of the synthesis of the major surfactant phospholipids in the lung is still a matter of controversy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the synthesis of PG is stimulated by the presence of surfactant lipids, whereas PI synthesis is suppressed by them.
the PI to PG switch-over is regulated by the availability of glycerol 3-phosphate (G3P) and the relative activity of phosphatidic acid (PA) phosphatase and phosphatidyl glycerol kinase.
we have found that PI is the precursor of PG and that PI synthesis is down-regulated by the presence of PG.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many different ways to make phosphatidylserine.
there are two different pathways to the synthesis of PI and PG.
